**A question to start with**

Imagine the same drink offered in two different rooms, with different words and different gestures. This chapter asks how to investigate everything around the liquid without confusing those influences with its chemistry.

**As you read:** Follow warmth → ritual → expectation → the context map. Keep asking what a comparison holds constant and what it changes.

<!-- reading-fold:start -->
:::::::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Earlier introduction and reading notes"}


Chemistry explains why a leaf can wake you. History explains why that leaf is cheap in your cupboard. This chapter asks what else rides along in the mug: **warmth**, **ritual**, and **expectation**.

Hold three kitchen pictures. One is a cozy mug in the hand while you meet someone new. Another is a short, familiar brew sequence—measure, watch, wait—before a hard task. A third is a label or a vessel that says "specialty" versus "just bag." The same compounds can share the cup with all three. The effects are tints, not destiny, and replication humility stays on the page.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Words to know on this journey"}
- **Anterior insular cortex** — the brain area that handles both body temperature and feelings like trust or empathy.
- **Embodied cognition** — the claim that body feelings, such as warmth, can shape social judgments.
- **Error-related negativity (ERN)** — a quick brain "oops" signal after mistakes. In some studies, predictable rituals can blunt related anxiety responses.
- **Expectation / label cues** — belief about what the drink is, shaped by price, packaging, vessel, or story.
:::

## Carry-forward into Decisions

If you take only one sentence into [Chapter 5](../module-05/index.qmd), take this one: **context can shape how a given dose is experienced.** Temperature, ritual, and expectation may influence a response alongside caffeine and [L-theanine](../../glossary.qmd#l-theanine). When they could affect the outcome, decision studies should measure or control factors such as cup temperature and bitterness, and headlines should say what was actually held constant.
